strengths: The paper addresses a practically important image-editing problem: removing an object and its shadows or reflections while preserving unrelated content. Supervising object-conditioned attention and reusing it for background fusion provides a coherent, useful solution.

OBER is a substantial contribution: 2,715 captured training pairs, 10,000 simulated examples, separate object and effect annotations, and two evaluation sets. The combination supports research beyond conventional masked inpainting.

Table 1 provides strong empirical evidence across both the authors’ benchmark and external RORD data. ObjectClear achieves 32.98 dB on OBER-Test and 26.40 dB on RORD-Val, exceeding all evaluated baselines even when those receive object-effect masks. Improvements also extend to LPIPS and CLIP distance.

The evaluation includes eight baselines, two mask conditions, component ablations, and qualitative examples involving reflections and multiple objects. The 30-participant study further supports perceptual usefulness, with 90.29% and 84.69% preference against the PowerPaint and RORem alternatives, respectively.

Overall, the dataset and demonstrated editing improvements provide a stronger case for acceptance than rejection. The reservations concern attribution, the simulation formulation, and reproducibility rather than an absence of a supported contribution.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not fully distinguish improved removal from improved background copying. In Table 2, attention supervision adds 0.27 dB and simulated data adds 0.44 dB, whereas fusion adds 4.98 dB. Background preservation is valuable, but comparisons using equivalent background fusion for baselines supplied with object-effect masks, together with object-only and effect-only metrics, are needed to substantiate the claimed removal advantage separately.

The synthetic-data formulation is technically underspecified. Equation 1 corresponds to a black-overlay model for darkening effects, but the foreground effect colors used in subsequent alpha blending are not defined. It is not a general alpha-recovery equation: brightening effects can produce negative values, and RGB-channel handling is unspecified. Consequently, the claimed accurate RGBA extraction and physically realistic compositing are not established as written.

Evidence for precise effect localization is incomplete. Figure 6 reports recall of 0.97 without precision, IoU, a threshold, or a clearly specified evaluation population; recall alone cannot exclude overly broad masks. Table 2 also does not isolate multi-object synthesis, reflection supplementation, or fusion without attention supervision, limiting attribution of the claimed capabilities.

Several details needed for reproduction are missing: the relative weighting of diffusion and mask losses, attention aggregation and normalization, the conversion from attention to the fusion mask, Gaussian-blur settings, and the image-difference threshold for annotation. Scene/object separation between training and testing, and exclusion of test foregrounds from synthetic-data construction, are not documented. Appendix B’s 50 model-generated reflection pairs are also not clearly reconciled with the reported dataset counts.

The novelty is primarily an effective integration of existing conditioning, attention-supervision, and blending ideas, as the manuscript itself acknowledges. Broader claims should therefore be calibrated to the evidence: OBER-Wild’s ReMOVE gain over the strongest baseline is only 0.0015 without uncertainty estimates, and insertion, movement, and coarse-mask robustness are demonstrated qualitatively rather than established through systematic evaluation.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: removing an object together with its shadows and reflections while preserving unrelated content. Combining supervised object-effect attention with attention-guided fusion is a coherent and useful approach.

OBER represents a substantial data contribution: 2,715 captured training pairs, 10,000 simulated pairs, separate object and effect annotations, and two evaluation sets. These annotations support more explicit effect localization than ordinary object-removal supervision.

Table 1 provides strong empirical evidence across an external benchmark and the proposed benchmark. ObjectClear achieves 26.40 dB PSNR on RORD-Val and 32.98 dB on OBER-Test, with substantial LPIPS improvements. Evaluating baselines with both object-only and object-effect masks strengthens the comparisons.

Qualitative examples support successful shadow and reflection removal, including some multi-object scenes. The supplementary 30-participant study reports 90.29% and 84.69% preference against the PowerPaint and RORem comparison groups, respectively, providing evidence beyond reconstruction metrics.
Overall, the useful dataset, substantial measured improvements, and supporting visual and human evaluations favor weak acceptance, despite meaningful limitations in attribution and reproducibility.
weaknesses: The experiments do not fully isolate the methodological contribution. Table 2 shows that adding attention supervision improves PSNR from 27.29 to 27.56, whereas fusion increases it from 28.00 to 32.98. There is no matched comparison with a separately predicted effect mask or equivalent background fusion applied to baselines, leaving uncertainty about the specific advantage of supervised cross-attention over simpler localization-and-compositing approaches.

Evidence for precise effect localization is incomplete. Figure 6 reports recall of approximately 0.97 without precision, IoU, or a clear thresholding protocol; broad masks can achieve high recall. Separate object-region and effect-region reconstruction metrics would better distinguish complete effect removal from the substantial gains due to background preservation.

The synthetic-data formulation is underspecified and not generally valid for all claimed effects. Equation 1 can produce negative alpha values where reflections brighten the background, and the foreground RGB values needed to make the subsequent compositing equation consistent are not defined. The equation resembles a multiplicative shadow approximation rather than a general RGBA decomposition, weakening the claim of accurate effect-preserving synthesis.

Important reproducibility details are missing, including the mask-loss weight relative to the diffusion loss, attention aggregation and normalization, fusion-mask conversion and blur parameters, and difference-mask thresholds. The dataset description also does not establish scene/object-disjoint splitting or clarify how the 50 pseudo-ground-truth reflection pairs in Appendix B enter the reported dataset counts.

The scope of several claims exceeds the evidence. The OBER-Wild ReMOVE advantage is small (0.9172 versus 0.9157), with no uncertainty estimates; multi-object and reflection-specific improvements are mainly qualitative. The appendix acknowledges failures on overlapping and long shadows, and the insertion/movement examples do not establish the conclusion's claim of consistently superior performance for those applications.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: removing an object and its shadows/reflections while preserving unrelated image content. Supervising object-conditioned attention with effect masks and reusing that attention for inference-time blending is a coherent, useful contribution, even though its individual components build on established techniques.

OBER is a meaningful dataset contribution: 2,715 captured training pairs, 10,000 simulated pairs, separate object/effect annotations, and two evaluation sets. The multi-object synthesis and explicit effect supervision extend beyond ordinary object-pasting datasets.

Table 1 provides strong empirical evidence across an external benchmark and the proposed benchmarks. ObjectClear achieves 26.40 dB PSNR and 0.0802 LPIPS on RORD-Val, and 32.98 dB and 0.0352 on OBER-Test. Evaluating baselines with both object-only and object-effect masks is a valuable comparison that gives competing methods access to the effects requiring removal.

The qualitative examples support the numerical results, including shadows, reflections, and selective removal in multi-object scenes. The supplementary 30-participant study also favors ObjectClear over PowerPaint and RORem, including when those baselines receive effect masks. Together, these results support weak acceptance despite the attribution and reproducibility concerns below.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not sufficiently separate removal quality from background copying. In Table 2, attention supervision improves PSNR from 27.29 to 27.56, simulated data increases it to 28.00, and fusion supplies the largest gain, to 32.98. Background preservation is a legitimate contribution, but object-only and effect-only evaluation, plus equivalent blending controls for baselines given effect masks, would clarify how much advantage comes from better removal rather than postprocessing. The present results support the full system more strongly than the claimed decoupling mechanism.

The synthetic-data formulation is technically underspecified. Equation 1's alpha = (Igt − Iin)/(Igt + epsilon) corresponds to a black attenuation layer under a simple shadow model, but the paper does not explain how effect-region colors in Ioe are constructed for the subsequent alpha blend. The expression can also yield negative values for brightening effects and channel-dependent values for RGB inputs. This does not invalidate the demonstrated system, but it limits confidence in the claimed physically realistic RGBA extraction and its reproducibility.

The evidence for precise effect localization is incomplete. Figure 6 reports approximately 0.97 recall without precision, IoU, a binarization threshold, or a clear evaluation population; recall alone cannot establish selective localization. Separate effect-region measurements would be particularly informative because object pixels can dominate the combined mask. The acknowledged failures on overlapping and long shadows are not quantified.

Several consequential implementation and dataset details are missing: the relative weighting of diffusion and mask losses, visual-token and attention aggregation details, attention-to-fusion-mask normalization or thresholding, Gaussian blur parameters, and the difference threshold used for annotations. The captured-data split is not explicitly described as scene/object-disjoint, and the foreground sources used for synthesis are not explicitly restricted to the training split. These are uncertainties, not evidence of leakage, but they limit reproducibility and interpretation of OBER-Test.

The breadth of comparisons is useful, but some closely related effect-aware methods discussed in the paper, such as LayerDecomp and OmniPaint, lack quantitative comparisons or a clear explanation of availability constraints. On OBER-Wild, the ReMOVE improvement over the strongest baseline is small (0.9172 versus 0.9157), with no uncertainty estimates. The user study strengthens the practical case, although it covers only two baselines and leaves presentation randomization and vote aggregation insufficiently specified.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful and challenging editing problem: removing an object and its shadows/reflections while preserving unrelated content. Supervising target-conditioned cross-attention and reusing it for background fusion forms a coherent, practical contribution.

Quantitative support is substantial. On RORD-Val, ObjectClear achieves 26.24 dB PSNR versus 24.38 for the strongest baseline; on OBER-Test, it achieves 33.04 versus 29.06. Supplementary evaluations on OmniPaint-Bench, OmniEraser-Bench, and effect-free MULAN samples strengthen the evidence for generalization beyond the authors' dataset.

The evaluation includes useful fairness controls: object-only and object-effect input masks, plus background blending with ground-truth effect masks for several baselines in Table 7. ObjectClear remains stronger in that experiment despite using predicted masks.

The supplementary user study provides complementary perceptual evidence: 30 participants prefer ObjectClear over OmniPaint in 70.33% of comparisons. Qualitative examples demonstrate preservation of nearby objects and removal of both shadows and reflections.

OBER contributes paired captured images, separate object/effect annotations, and scalable synthetic training data. The reported 1.63-second inference time at 512×512 also supports practical usefulness. Together, the dataset and consistently supported system improvements favor acceptance despite the reservations below.
weaknesses: Important implementation details remain unspecified. The manuscript does not adequately define the mask-loss weighting, visual-token configuration, attention aggregation/normalization for fusion, or Gaussian-blur settings. SVDS lacks an explicit update rule and noise schedule explaining how different denoising strengths and background reinjection are implemented. These omissions materially limit reproducibility.

The synthetic-data formulation needs stronger technical justification. Equation 1 gives a shadow-style intensity ratio that can become negative for brightening or reflection effects; channel handling, clipping, and construction of the foreground RGB values used in compositing are unclear. Consequently, the claim of physically plausible general object-effect compositing is stronger than the stated formulation supports. The supplementary pseudo-paired reflection data helps empirically but does not resolve this formulation.

Precise effect localization is incompletely evaluated. Figure 6 reports recall near 0.97 without precision, IoU, or a clearly specified threshold and evaluation population. Recall alone cannot establish avoidance of unrelated-region removal. Effect-only reconstruction metrics and localization measurements would better support the central claim, particularly given the overlapping-shadow failures acknowledged in Figure 17.

The ablations establish the usefulness of the combined system more clearly than the distinctiveness of ATA. In Table 2, ATA adds 0.27 dB PSNR, whereas fusion adds 4.73 dB. There is no matched comparison against a separately supervised effect-mask predictor or simpler localization approach. Table 7 partially addresses blending-related concerns, but omits the strongest recent competitors, including OmniPaint and GeoRemover.

Dataset provenance and split safeguards are insufficiently documented: the paper does not explicitly establish scene/object separation or confirm that synthetic foreground sources exclude captured test samples. The additional 50 selected reflection pairs are also not reconciled clearly with the dataset totals. These are uncertainties, not evidence of leakage. Minor claim calibration is also needed: ObjectClear trails OmniPaint on OBER-Wild ReMOVE† and OmniEraser-Bench DINO, despite some blanket superiority statements.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful and challenging editing problem: removing an object and its shadows/reflections while preserving unrelated content. Supervising object-conditioned attention and reusing it for background fusion is a coherent design. The visual comparisons show meaningful improvements in effect removal and background preservation.

The empirical support extends beyond the authors’ dataset. Table 1 reports 26.24 dB on RORD-Val versus 24.38 for the strongest PSNR baseline, and 33.04 dB on OBER-Test versus 29.06. The appendix adds OmniPaint-Bench, OmniEraser-Bench, and 500 effect-free MULAN examples, with improvements on most metrics. This breadth supports usefulness and generalization.

The evaluation includes valuable controls and complementary evidence. Table 7 gives baselines ground-truth object-effect masks for background blending, yet ObjectClear remains ahead of the included methods. The 30-participant user study reports 70.33% preference over OmniPaint and 78.90% over OmniEraser, supporting perceptual benefits beyond reconstruction metrics.

OBER is a potentially useful dataset contribution: 2,715 captured training pairs, 10,000 simulated pairs, separate object/effect annotations, and two evaluation sets. Table 2 supports incremental benefits from attention supervision, simulated data, fusion, and spatially varying denoising. The reported 1.63-second inference time versus OmniPaint’s 9.42 seconds on an A100 also suggests practical value.

Overall, the supported system and dataset contributions favor weak acceptance. Although the methodological novelty is primarily in integrating established ingredients, the broad quantitative evaluation, qualitative evidence, and user study provide a stronger case for acceptance than rejection.
weaknesses: The attribution of improvements to precise effect understanding is incomplete. In Table 2, attention supervision improves PSNR from 27.29 to 27.56, whereas fusion increases it from 28.04 to 32.77. Background preservation is a legitimate contribution, but whole-image metrics do not isolate reconstruction or effect-removal quality. Figure 6 reports approximately 0.97 mask recall without precision, IoU, or effect-only accuracy; broad masks can obtain high recall. Table 7 partly addresses the blending concern, but omits the particularly relevant OmniPaint and OmniEraser baselines.

Important implementation details remain unspecified. The manuscript does not clearly state the relative weighting of diffusion and mask losses, the aggregation and normalization of visual-token attention into a fusion mask, or the exact SVDS reinjection rule and scheduler. These details materially affect reproduction, particularly because a denoising-strength change from 0.99 to 1.0 is scheduler-dependent. The claim that full noise discards all input information is also too broad: the model remains conditioned on the input image and object embedding.

The simulation pipeline needs a more precise technical account. Equation 1 estimates effect opacity using (Igt − Iin)/(Igt + epsilon), which is compatible with a black shadow layer under restrictive assumptions, but the corresponding foreground-layer construction is not specified. Bright reflections can produce negative values, and RGB ratios need not define a scalar alpha. Clipping, channel handling, and foreground values are therefore consequential omissions. The separately described 50 manually selected reflection pseudo-pairs help explain reflection training, but do not establish the claimed physical plausibility of the general compositing procedure.

Dataset quality and separation are insufficiently documented. Thresholded image differences may include exposure changes or misalignment and miss faint effects, yet annotation accuracy is not quantified. The paper also does not specify scene/object-disjoint splitting or explicitly confirm that test foregrounds are excluded from synthetic training generation. This is an uncertainty about the protocol, not evidence of leakage. External benchmark results mitigate, but do not eliminate, this concern.

Some claims exceed the reported evidence. OmniPaint scores higher on OBER-Wild ReMOVE† (0.8656 versus 0.8470), and on OmniEraser-Bench DINO distance (0.0213 versus 0.0230), contradicting the appendix’s claim of superiority across all metrics. The modified ReMOVE metric lacks validation against human judgments. The acknowledged failures on overlapping effects also qualify claims of precise object-specific disentanglement; their frequency is not quantified. These limitations warrant narrower claims, although they do not negate the overall empirical contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important editing problem: removing an object and its shadows or reflections while preserving unrelated content. Supervised target-aware attention provides a coherent connection between effect localization, removal, and background fusion.

The empirical evidence is substantial. Table 1 reports 33.04 dB PSNR on OBER-Test versus 29.06 for OmniPaint, and 26.24 on RORD-Val versus 24.38 for GeoRemover. Additional evaluations on OmniPaint-Bench, OmniEraser-Bench, and MULAN support generalization beyond the authors’ benchmark.

The appendix strengthens the comparison through a 30-participant user study and an experiment giving competing methods ground-truth effect masks for background blending. The latter helps demonstrate that improvements are not solely attributable to preserving background pixels.

OBER is a useful dataset contribution, combining 2,715 captured training pairs and 10,000 simulated pairs with separate object and effect annotations. The qualitative examples demonstrate convincing removal of shadows, reflections, and selected interacting objects.

The ablations support the practical value of the components, particularly attention-guided fusion. Together with the external evaluations, these results favor acceptance despite limitations in attribution and reproducibility.
weaknesses: The distinct contribution of the attention mechanism is only partially isolated. In Table 2, adding ATA improves PSNR from 27.29 to 27.56, whereas fusion improves it from 28.04 to 32.77. There is no comparison with a separate effect-mask predictor or an alternative supervised localization mechanism, leaving the necessity of attention-based localization insufficiently established.

Effect-localization accuracy is assessed primarily through recall, reported as 0.97 in Figure 6. Without precision or IoU, this does not establish precise localization: oversized masks can achieve high recall while allowing unwanted edits. Region-specific object and effect reconstruction metrics would also better separate removal quality from background preservation.

The synthetic-data formulation needs clarification. Equation 1’s effect alpha assumes a darkening relationship and can become negative for brightening effects; the foreground RGB used with this alpha is not sufficiently specified to verify the compositing model. Matching shadow directions and selecting flat placement regions also do not establish the claimed physical consistency of lighting and geometry.

Several implementation details remain underspecified, including the relative weighting of mask and diffusion losses, attention-token/head aggregation and normalization for fusion, and the exact scheduler and reinjection procedure for spatially varying denoising. The dataset description also does not explicitly establish that all foregrounds used in simulation exclude held-out captured examples; this is an unresolved split-protocol detail, not evidence of leakage.

Some claims exceed the reported results. ObjectClear trails OmniPaint on OBER-Wild ReMOVE†, and Table 5 does not support the statement that it wins every metric: OmniPaint has better DINO distance on OmniEraser-Bench. Figure 17 also demonstrates failures on overlapping effects, qualifying claims of precise removal in complex scenes. These limitations temper the recommendation without outweighing the broader empirical contribution.
